title: Convolutional Neural Networks
oneLiner: A CNN slides small learned pattern detectors across an image, then combines what they find, layer after layer, from edges to whole objects.

what.html:
A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a network built for images and other grid-shaped data. Instead of connecting every pixel to every neuron, it uses small filters (e.g. 3×3 patches of weights) that slide across the image looking for one pattern each: a vertical edge, a corner, a patch of fur.

Everyday versionLooking for Waldo, you don't memorise the whole page. You scan with a small mental template ("red-and-white stripes") everywhere on the page. A CNN does the same with many templates at once, and its later layers look for combinations: stripes + glasses + hat = Waldo.

Early layers find edges, middle layers find textures and parts, deep layers recognise objects. All the filters are learned from data.

why.html:
• Images are huge. A 224×224 colour photo has 150,528 numbers; a fully connected layer on it would need hundreds of millions of weights.
  • Patterns are local: an edge only involves nearby pixels.
  • Patterns can appear anywhere: a cat's ear is a cat's ear in any corner, so one detector reused everywhere is enough.
  • Vision is hierarchical: objects are built from parts built from edges.

how.title: The overall shape of a CNN
how.html: Input image → [convolution → ReLU → pooling] repeated → flatten → dense layers → softmax. The picture shrinks (32×32 → 14×14 → 5×5) while the number of feature channels grows (3 → 6 → 16), until a small vector of features feeds the classifier.

how.title: Convolution: slide and score
how.html: Place the 3×3 filter on the top-left of the image, multiply each pair of overlapping numbers, add them up: that's one output value. Shift by one pixel and repeat. The grid of results is a feature map: high where the image looks like the filter. Use 64 filters and you get 64 feature maps stacked into a block.

how.title: How far can a neuron see?
how.html: A neuron's receptive field is the patch of the original image that can affect it. One 3×3 layer sees 3×3 pixels; two layers see 5×5; three see 7×7. Stacking small filters is cheaper than one big filter and gives the same view, with extra non-linearity in between.

how.title: Filters are learned, not designed
how.html: The 9 numbers in each filter are weights, trained by backpropagation like any other. Start random; after training, first-layer filters look like edge detectors at different angles. Because each filter is reused at every position, its gradient adds up contributions from all positions.

how.title: Padding, stride and dilation
how.html: Padding adds a border of zeros so the output keeps its size and edge pixels get attention. Stride is the step size: stride 2 halves the output (cheap downsampling). Dilation spreads the filter's taps apart to see a wider area with the same 9 weights. Output size = (input + 2·padding − kernel) / stride + 1.

how.title: Colour and many channels
how.html: A colour image has 3 channels, so each filter is 3×3×3: it looks at all channels at once and adds them up into one map. 64 filters → 64 output channels. Deeper networks typically halve the picture size and double the channels at each stage (224×224×3 → … → 14×14×512).

how.title: Pooling: shrink and keep the strongest
how.html: Max pooling splits the map into 2×2 windows and keeps the biggest value of each: the map shrinks 4× in area, the strongest detections survive, and small shifts matter less. Average pooling keeps the mean instead. Pooling has no weights to learn.

how.title: 1×1 convolutions and bottlenecks
how.html: A 1×1 filter doesn't look at neighbours: it mixes the channels at each pixel, like a tiny dense layer applied everywhere. Squeezing 256 channels down to 64 before an expensive 5×5 filter and back up afterwards cuts the weights about 12-fold: the bottleneck trick behind Inception and ResNet.

how.title: ReLU, dense layer, softmax
how.html: After each convolution, ReLU sets negatives to zero (simple, fast, keeps gradients alive). At the end, the feature block is flattened and a dense layer combines everything into class scores, which softmax turns into probabilities. Dense layers hold most of the weights; global average pooling is a lighter alternative.

how.title: Counting parameters
how.html: A conv layer has (kernel × kernel × input channels + 1) × filters weights, no matter how big the image is. 64 filters of 5×5 on an RGB image: 4,864 weights. Pooling: zero. That's why CNNs are so much smaller than dense networks on images.

how.title: Design patterns
how.html: Successful networks reuse a few ideas: shrink the picture while adding channels; repeat a standard block; add skip connections; use bottlenecks; look at several scales at once. Pick depth by task, data and compute: a few layers for digits, 50–150 for ImageNet-scale problems. Start simple, grow if underfitting.

how.title: Landmark networks
how.html: LeNet-5 (1998) read digits. AlexNet (2012) won ImageNet with ReLU, dropout, augmentation and GPUs. VGG (2014) used only 3×3 filters, 16–19 layers. Network in Network introduced 1×1 convolutions and global average pooling. GoogLeNet/Inception (2014) ran 1×1, 3×3 and 5×5 filters side by side with 1×1 bottlenecks: 22 layers with only 5M weights.

how.title: ResNet: learn the change, not the whole thing
how.html: Plain networks got worse on training data when made very deep. ResNet adds a shortcut that passes the input straight to the output of each block: output = F(input) + input. The block only learns the correction. Gradients get a highway back through the shortcuts, so 50–152-layer networks train well.

how.title: Transfer learning
how.html: Don't start from scratch: take a network trained on ImageNet's 1.2M images and reuse it. Small, similar dataset → freeze it and train only a new classifier. More data → fine-tune all layers with a small learning rate. Different domain → fine-tune later layers, or train from scratch if you have lots of data.

how.title: What CNNs are used for, and common traps
how.html: Classification, object detection (YOLO, Faster R-CNN), segmentation (U-Net, DeepLab), faces, style transfer, super-resolution, plus 1-D convolutions on audio, text and time series. Normalise and augment images, use batch norm and dropout, watch validation curves, and reach for pre-trained models first.

demo.html: Press Step to slide the slides' diagonal filter across the 6×6 image and watch each output being computed. You'll find two 3s: the same pattern in two places, found by one shared filter. Then switch to stride 3 (2×2 output) or padding 1 (6×6 output), or try the vertical-line filter with ReLU.

example.html:
Face detection: layer 1 edges → layer 2 eyes, nose, mouth → layer 3 whole faces. ImageNet: AlexNet's 15.3% top-5 error in 2012 fell to 3.6% with ResNet in 2015. Medical imaging, autonomous driving, satellite imagery use segmentation networks such as U-Net.

Supplementary Telecom field teams photograph antennas and cabinets; a fine-tuned ResNet flags corrosion, loose cables or wrong tilt. Spectrograms of radio signals are images too, so CNNs classify interference types from them.

misunderstandings: Each position in the image has its own filter weights.
One filter is shared across all positions; that's why CNNs are small.
Pooling layers learn which values to keep.
They have no parameters; max or average is a fixed rule.
Stacks of 3×3 filters see the same area with fewer weights and more non-linearity.
Plain deep nets train worse; depth needs skip connections, batch norm and enough data.
It mixes channels and cheaply reduces their number (bottlenecks).
takeaways: Convolution slides a small learned filter over the input; one filter = one feature map; weights are shared across positions.
Output size = ⌊(n + 2p − k)/s⌋ + 1; parameters = (k·k·C_in + 1)·C_out; pooling has none.
Stack conv → ReLU → pool: spatial size shrinks, channels grow, receptive fields widen from edges to objects.
1×1 bottlenecks, multi-scale Inception modules and residual connections made deep CNNs efficient and trainable.
Use transfer learning from pre-trained networks; augment data and regularise to avoid overfitting.
thirty: A CNN processes images with small learned filters that slide across the input, so each neuron only looks at a local patch and the same weights are reused everywhere. Each filter produces a feature map showing where its pattern appears. Layers of convolution and ReLU, interleaved with pooling or strided convolutions, shrink the image while increasing the number of channels, so later layers see larger regions and detect more complex things: edges, then textures, then object parts and whole objects. A dense or global-average-pooling head with softmax gives class probabilities. Architectures evolved from LeNet and AlexNet to VGG, Inception with 1×1 bottlenecks, and ResNet with skip connections that make 100-plus-layer networks trainable, and in practice we usually fine-tune a pre-trained network.
